title: Aldehydes & ketones
examples: What is the difference between aldehydes and ketones?
How do I test for aldehydes in a lab?
Can you explain the mechanism of nucleophilic addition?

explain.say: Today we will look at aldehydes and ketones.
Aldehydes have a hydrogen atom attached to the carbonyl carbon.
Ketones have two carbon groups attached to the carbonyl carbon.
Aldehydes react with nucleophiles through nucleophilic addition.
Tollens' test uses silver ions to test for aldehydes.
Fehling's test uses copper ions to test for aldehydes.

faq.q: How can I tell if a compound is an aldehyde or a ketone?
faq.a: You can check the structure to see if it has hydrogen on the carbonyl carbon. If it does, it is likely an aldehyde.
asks: What is the difference between the two groups?
Which group has an H attached to the C=O?

faq.q: What does a positive result mean in these tests?
faq.a: A positive result means the specific functional group, like an aldehyde, is present in the sample.
asks: What does the silver mirror show?
Does a positive test confirm the group?

faq.q: Are these tests specific enough for sure identification?
faq.a: These tests are highly indicative, but confirming structure often requires multiple tests or advanced techniques.
asks: Can I use these tests for all carbonyls?
Are there exceptions to these rules?

faq.q: What is the role of the nucleophile in the reaction?
faq.a: The nucleophile is an electron-rich species that attacks the electron-deficient carbonyl carbon.
asks: Why does the nucleophile attack the carbon?
What makes the carbonyl carbon electrophilic?

faq.q: Do ketones also undergo nucleophilic addition?
faq.a: Ketones can undergo addition, but aldehydes are generally more reactive due to less steric hindrance.

facts: Aldehydes have the general formula R-CHO.
Ketones have the general formula R-CO-R.
Tollens' test gives a silver mirror with aldehydes.
Fehling's test gives a brick-red precipitate with aldehydes.

quiz.say: A compound that gives a positive result with Tollens' reagent is most likely a:
quiz.why: Tollens' reagent specifically reduces aldehydes, forming the characteristic silver mirror.

wrong.1: Ketones are generally less reactive towards mild oxidizing agents like Tollens' reagent.
wrong.2: Carboxylic acids require different conditions and reagents for detection.
wrong.3: Alcohols are not aldehydes and do not produce a silver mirror with this test.

quiz.say: If a sample gives a positive result with Fehling's solution, the compound is likely a:
quiz.why: Fehling's solution contains copper ions that are reduced to form a brick-red precipitate only by aldehydes.

wrong.1: Ketones lack the necessary hydrogen atom on the carbonyl carbon for this specific reaction.
wrong.2: Primary amines react with different reagents, not Fehling's solution.
wrong.3: Ethers are stable compounds and do not react with Fehling's reagent.

options.say: The test results are always the same for both.

options.say: Aldehydes have hydrogen on the carbonyl carbon.
